prompt: The light on Harlow turns yellow. Left gets you home in nine minutes. Right is the long way, past the reservoir, where nothing has ever happened to anybody.

risk.description: A minivan you did not see had the same idea about the same yellow light.

prompt: {{cast:dev}}'s parents are in Sedona. There will be a bathtub of something blue in it. {{cast:best friend}} says they will go if you go.

risk.description: The trampoline was not designed for this. Neither was your collarbone.

setting: A Thursday in April, the garden centre car park.
prompt: The garden center is hiring. Eleven dollars an hour to water things and watch a man named Rick describe his divorce.

setting: Registration week, the guidance office corridor.
prompt: Six Saturdays of test prep, or six Saturdays of the marching band, which you are told will matter to you forever and which you will remember in flashes.
{{cast:casey}} has been leaving a very specific amount of space next to them at lunch for three weeks.

setting: Saturday morning, a driveway two streets over.
prompt: A 1998 Corolla, $1,600, described by its owner as 'basically immortal.' It is the color of an old bandage.
The chemistry final is tomorrow and someone has a photograph of it. You did not ask for the photograph. It is simply on your phone now.

risk.description: Mr. Alvarez recognizes his own typo in your answer. The word 'academic dishonesty' enters your permanent file and your parents' vocabulary.

setting: The last week of August, the field behind the school.
prompt: Varsity tryouts. Coach Bell says you have the frame for it. Coach Bell says this to everyone with a frame.

risk.description: Your knee makes a sound the trainer describes only as 'yeah.'

prompt: Behind the auditorium, someone holds out a cigarette like it is a small, glowing invitation to a different personality.

setting: The final day of term, everyone signing everything.
prompt: Last summer before everything gets scheduled forever. There is a hospital volunteer program, and there is the reservoir.

setting: Late March, the kitchen table, two envelopes already opened.
beat: Your mother has read both of them twice and put them back exactly as they were, squared to the edge of the table, the way she does with things that frighten her.
dialogue: "Whichever one," she says, "don't pick it because of us."
prompt: Two envelopes. Brackwood College, private, $58,000 a year, ivy grown deliberately. State, $11,000 a year, and a parking problem.

setting: The library computer bank on a Thursday, the registration deadline at noon, a queue forming behind you.
beat: The starting salaries are $74,000 for computer science and $41,000 for philosophy, according to the pamphlet nobody reads.
dialogue: The girl waiting behind you says you can change it later. Nobody changes it later.
prompt: Declare the major that pays for the life, or the one that explains it, and decide which person you can stand being at forty.

setting: Move-in day, a room with two of everything.
prompt: Your roommate {{cast:sam}} has opinions about music, a fake ID, and a bottle of gin they refer to as 'the emergency.' {{cast:sam}} wants to be friends.

setting: November, the study-abroad noticeboard outside the library.
prompt: A semester in Lisbon. It costs $9,000 you would have to borrow and it is, everyone agrees, the sort of thing you only get to do now.

setting: Careers fair, third hour, the free pens long gone.
prompt: An unpaid internship at a firm whose name opens doors, or $19/hour at a warehouse whose name opens a loading bay.

setting: A borrowed office above a barber's on a Tuesday night, three chairs, a whiteboard, somebody's dinner going cold.
beat: They are offering ten percent of the company and $24,000 a year, with eight months of runway raised.
dialogue: One of them says they cannot do it without you, and means it entirely.
prompt: Three semesters from a degree, or a bill-splitting app with your name already on the deck. Decide which story you want to tell about yourself.

risk.description: BillSplit is acquired for parts, and your parts are worth something.

setting: Two in the morning, somebody's floor, four laptops open.
prompt: A guy from your dorm has moved $4,000 into a coin named after a frog. He is extremely calm about it, which is the frightening part.

risk.description: The frog goes up. You sell near the top, which will make you insufferable for a decade.

setting: March, a fire escape, the party audible below.
prompt: {{cast:sam}} kisses you on a fire escape in March and asks, without much preamble, whether this is a thing now.

setting: A Friday, two offer letters, both expiring Monday.
beat: You have read them enough times to have them by heart, which has not helped.
dialogue: "Take the money," says your father. "Take the money," says everyone.
prompt: Two offers. Ninety-four thousand at an insurance company with a wellness room. Sixty-one thousand at a startup that pays partly in a number on a spreadsheet.

risk.description: The spreadsheet number becomes a real number. Not a life-changing one. A car-changing one.

setting: September, a city you have visited exactly once, for a rained-out weekend you keep editing into a good one.
beat: The job pays $118,000; the rent is $2,400 against the $1,100 you pay now, and the lease needs signing Thursday.
dialogue: Mom says four hours is nothing, in the voice she uses for things that are not nothing.
prompt: Do you become someone who left and built a life from scratch, or someone who stayed close and never had to find out?

setting: A parking garage on the fourth level, eleven at night.
beat: {{cast:sam}} has been holding the ring since the restaurant and has clearly rehearsed this badly.
dialogue: "The acoustics are incredible up here," {{cast:sam}} says, kneeling anyway.
prompt: {{cast:sam}} proposes in a parking garage, which {{cast:sam}} insists is romantic because of the acoustics. {{cast:sam}} has been drinking, but {{cast:sam}} has been drinking for eleven years, so this tells you nothing.

setting: Onboarding week, a laminated folder you will never open again.
prompt: HR needs your retirement allocation by Friday. There is a slider. Nobody will ever explain the slider to you.

risk.description: A decade of quiet compounding does what nobody in the building expected.

prompt: The gym is $54 a month and eleven minutes away. You have driven past it 400 times.

setting: A Tuesday at the good restaurant, chosen for being loud, somewhere between the salad and the check.
beat: You have been circling this for two years; the first year alone costs about $12,000, and you both know it.
dialogue: They say the two of you keep saying next year, and they have stopped believing it.
prompt: Do you become somebody's parent starting now, at this table, or stay the couple whose plans are always scheduled for next year?

setting: A second viewing, Saturday, the agent waiting in the car.
beat: You have already worked out where the table would go, which is how they get you.
dialogue: "There's interest," the agent says, from the doorway, to nobody.
prompt: A house with a cracked driveway and a kitchen from 1987. The mortgage is a number you will say out loud to people for thirty years.

setting: Sunday night, the kitchen table, everything else cleared off.
prompt: You could build the thing on nights and weekends. Sleep is, statistically, optional for about four months.

risk.description: Somebody links to it. Then somebody with money links to it.

setting: Six weeks after the surgery, the bathroom cabinet.
prompt: The knee surgery left you with a bottle of thirty and a refill you did not ask for. There are nine left and it is Tuesday, which you know because you have started noticing which day it is.

risk.description: You run out early and the pharmacy will not budge, and the two days that follow are their own kind of education.

setting: Six on a Sunday, the living room, everyone already seated.
beat: Your sister has printed something and is holding it face down on her knee, and nobody has taken their coat off, which tells you how long they intend to stay.
dialogue: "We're not leaving," she says. "That's the whole plan, that's it."
prompt: Everyone is in the living room at 6pm on a Sunday, which has never once happened by accident. Your sister has printed something out.

setting: A church hall on a Wednesday, the good coffee for once.
prompt: Fourteen months. Somebody at the meeting asks if you would speak next week, and you notice you have opinions about what you would say.

setting: The Friday before audit season, your desk, everyone else gone.
beat: Eleven months of a gap you found by accident, now thirty-four thousand wide.
dialogue: "Monday, then," the auditor had said on the phone, pleasantly.
prompt: The expense system has a gap in it you found by accident eleven months ago, and you have been walking through the gap ever since. It is now $34,000 wide. Audit season starts Monday.

risk.description: The auditor is twenty-six, thorough, and has nothing else on her desk. The word 'felony' is used in a room with a window.

setting: A conference room with one window, your lawyer's third coffee.
beat: Eighteen months is the offer, and he says it the way he has said it many times.
dialogue: "A jury gets shown the spreadsheet," he says. "Juries hate spreadsheets."
prompt: Your lawyer says eighteen months is the offer and that the alternative is a jury who will be shown a spreadsheet. He says it the way people say things they have said many times.

risk.description: The jury takes four hours. The sentence is longer than the offer was.

setting: A reentry office above a laundrette, two chairs and a kettle.
beat: Two jobs on the desk between you, and one of them has a box on the form.
dialogue: "Bayonne won't ask," he says. "Newark will. That's the whole difference."
prompt: The box on the application is a checkbox and the checkbox is not optional. A man from a reentry program says there is a contractor in Bayonne who does not ask, and a facilities job in Newark where you would have to say it out loud in an interview.
rightLabel: Take the job that won't ask

setting: Sunday afternoon, the phone face-up on the arm of the sofa.
prompt: The sportsbook app gave you $200 free and you turned it into $1,400 in a weekend, which felt less like luck than like a skill nobody had told you about.

risk.description: A parlay lands that should not have landed, and the number on the screen is bigger than a month of your salary.

setting: Thursday, three weeks in, a phone you have stopped answering.
beat: Sixty-one thousand across four apps and one man who does not use apps.
dialogue: "I'm not in a rush," Terrence says, which is the part that frightens you.
prompt: You are $61,000 down across four apps and one man named Terrence who does not use apps. Terrence is polite. Terrence has been polite for three weeks now.

risk.description: Terrence stops being polite in a parking structure on a Thursday.

setting: Half eleven, the pub car park, keys already in your hand.
beat: Four drinks and eleven minutes of road you could drive in your sleep.
dialogue: "Leave it," someone says from the doorway. "Get it in the morning."
prompt: You are four drinks in and the car is right there and the drive is eleven minutes on roads you could do asleep, which is a thought you notice having.

risk.description: The stop is routine until it is not, and the phrase 'driving while intoxicated' enters your record, your insurance, and every background check for the next decade.

prompt: Someone has written something about you on the inside of a locker door, and three people have already told you about it kindly.

setting: Last period Friday, the classroom emptying out.
prompt: Ms. Okafor keeps you after class to say she has recommended you for something without asking first. It is four Saturdays and a bus ride, and she has clearly already told people you will do it.
Your cousin wants to borrow the car for two hours and has been vague about which two hours.

risk.description: The car comes back with a story attached and a dent that does not match the story.

setting: Wednesday, the group chat already deciding without you.
prompt: The Friday shift pays time and a half. The game is the last one anybody will care about, and everyone you know will be at it, and you will hear about it either way.
Dad has been in the shed since seven and the light is still on, and he has not asked for help, which is how he asks for help.
You are down to $14 and eleven days, and the bus fare home for the weekend is $31.

setting: Eleven at night, the twenty-four-hour floor of the library.
prompt: Two of the four names on the project have contributed nothing and one of them has a genuinely difficult year happening. The submission box closes at midnight and your name is on it too.

setting: Late April, exams done, everyone making plans loudly.
prompt: A friend has a spare room in another country for the summer and wants $400 for the whole thing. It is almost certainly a bad idea and it is almost certainly the last summer this is possible.
Your old landlord is keeping $900 of the deposit for damage that was there when you moved in, and you have a photograph proving it somewhere.

setting: February, the fourth save-the-date on the fridge.
prompt: The fourth wedding this year is in another country and you are in the photographs of all of them. The flights, the suit, the gift and the two nights come to more than your rent.

setting: Tuesday morning, the all-staff email still open.
prompt: The job you wanted went to the person you eat lunch with, who found out an hour before you did and has been avoiding the kitchen ever since.

setting: The reorganisation announced at nine, effective immediately.
prompt: Your new manager is thirty-one and keeps using the phrase 'legacy approach' in a tone that is not quite an insult. She is also, annoyingly, right about two of the four things.

setting: The house you grew up in, emptied into the hall in labelled boxes.
beat: Three weekends, forty years, and a piano nobody has played since 1998.
dialogue: "You were always the organised one," your sister says, not helping.
prompt: The house you grew up in has to be emptied in three weekends. There are forty years in it and your siblings have opinions about the piano, the photographs, and who did more.

setting: The consulting room, the scan already on the screen.
prompt: The knee has been going for two years and the surgeon says now is better than later, which is what they said about the other one.

setting: A Sunday, a car in the drive with the back seat full.
prompt: One of your children is coming home for what everyone is carefully calling a few months, with a car full of boxes and a job that ended in a way nobody has explained.

setting: A town hall held on Teams, the severance package explained in eleven slides, cameras optional and mostly off.
beat: Eleven months of salary, about $62,000, for anyone over fifty-five who volunteers, which is how they avoid choosing.
dialogue: The presenter says the word voluntary twice, once on the slide and once out loud.
prompt: Do you jump while jumping is paid for, or stay and find out whether they would ever have chosen you?

setting: The supermarket car park, her keys already in her hand.
prompt: Your daughter has started offering to drive whenever you are going anywhere further than the shops, and she has started offering before you have said where you are going.

risk.description: A junction you have used for thirty years arranges itself differently for a moment, and the other driver is fine.

prompt: The third funeral this year is two hours away and you would know perhaps four people there.

setting: Sunday lunch, after the plates have gone through.
prompt: A grandchild needs eleven thousand for a deposit and has asked in the specific way people ask when they have rehearsed it in the car outside.
You have started saying 'what?' as a reflex before people have finished, and someone has started repeating themselves before you ask.
There is a plot available on the site behind the church, and a waiting list of nine people who have each been waiting four years.
rightLabel: Let it go to someone else

setting: The solicitor's office, a form with more blank space than you expected.
beat: One of your children is named as executor and both of them will read this.
dialogue: "Equal shares?" she asks, pen down, entirely without opinion.
prompt: The solicitor wants to know what happens to everything, and the honest answer involves saying out loud which of your children you trust with it. They will read this document one day and know what you decided.

setting: Friday after school, the parking lot behind the auditorium. {{new:friend}} is leaning on a rusted Civic, holding a flyer for a weekend band that needs a merch t
prompt: The show runs until midnight, which means asking Dad, your father, for a late curfew he will almost certainly negotiate down to eleven.
Your sociology textbook is $187 new. The campus library has one copy with a three-week wait list.

setting: The break room at the coffee shop, a Wednesday in February. Your manager has taped a new shift schedule to the fridge.
prompt: You have been offered a third shift each week, which would bring in roughly $180 more per month but would land on the same morning as your stats lecture.
Your landlord is raising rent by $180 a month starting next month. Do you negotiate or start looking?

setting: The break room at your office, a Thursday in February. Someone has left a flyer for a 401(k) enrollment meeting on the counter.
prompt: HR is nudging everyone under 25 to enroll in the company 401(k). The match is three percent. You have other places you could use that money right now.
Your spouse left the thermostat at 62 degrees again. You have been quietly turning it back up for three years. Do you say something tonight or let it go?

setting: A Sunday in March, your mother's kitchen. She has a stack of unopened mail beside the toaster.
prompt: Mom, your mother, mentions casually that she has not looked at her bank statements since Dad started handling the finances. Dad, your father, had a minor health scare last fall. Do you offer to set her up with online banking, or leave well enough alone?
Your union newsletter arrives with an article on early retirement at 62. You are already 63. Do you read it anyway or recycle it unread?

setting: The break room at work, a Thursday in March. Someone has left a half-eaten birthday cake for a colleague who turned 40.
prompt: Your department head mentions, offhandedly, that a voluntary severance package is being offered to analysts over 60. The number is fourteen months of salary. Do you ask for the paperwork or say you are not interested?
A letter arrives from your bank offering a 'senior-friendly' investment product with guaranteed 18% annual returns. Do you request the information package?

setting: Your kitchen, a Thursday in March. The calendar on the wall has very few things written on it.
prompt: A community centre two miles away runs a Tuesday-Thursday woodworking class for retirees. It costs $40 a month and requires you to be somewhere twice a week.
Your phone's alarm has been going off at 6 a.m. for a week. You keep hitting snooze. Do you sign up for the early-morning tutoring session or sleep in?

setting: The school cafeteria, a Thursday in November. A hand-lettered sign on the drama department table says SPRING MUSICAL - AUDITIONS JAN 9.
prompt: You can actually carry a tune. Do you sign up for auditions, or decide your schedule is already stretched?
Your study group wants to split a $200 graphing calculator between four of you. Do you chip in or buy your own?

setting: Sunday afternoon, the common room of your dorm. Your mother has called for the third time this week.
prompt: You have been sitting on this. Do you call her back and talk it through honestly, or file the undecided paperwork and deal with the question later?
Your college email still forwards. A professor has sent a department newsletter you never asked to leave. Do you finally unsubscribe?

setting: A Friday happy hour, three weeks into the job. The marketing team is at the bar around the corner from the office.
prompt: Your manager, {{new:manager}}, mentions a weekend workshop on digital analytics - unpaid, but attendance gets noticed. You have plans you would have to cancel.
Your spouse left a real estate listing on the kitchen counter. No note, just the listing.

setting: A Thursday evening video call. Mom, your mother, is propped against the headboard of what appears to be a guest room that used to be yours.
prompt: She mentions, very casually, that she has been having trouble with her left knee and has not yet seen anyone about it.
Your phone buzzes at 11 p.m. on a school night. Do you answer?

setting: A Saturday afternoon in your driveway, late September. Dad, your father, has the hood of his car up and a socket set spread across a towel.
beat: He says he will teach you to change the oil and rotate the tires yourself, saving roughly $120 a year once you have a car.
dialogue: Dad says this is the kind of thing nobody teaches you and then charges you for your whole life.
prompt: You had plans with people from school. Do you stay and learn the basics from your father, or call it a dad-thing and head out?
Your phone dies at 11 p.m. and you can either borrow Mom's charger from her room or just go to sleep early for once.
A collection is going around homeroom for a teacher's retirement gift. You have $505. Do you chip in $20 or quietly pass the envelope along?

setting: The school gym, a Wednesday in November. Tryout sheets have been taped to the door since Monday.
prompt: The varsity coach is still accepting late sign-ups for the travel team, which means Saturday practices through March and an entry fee of $85. You have the money. Do you commit?
Your study hall period is forty minutes of nothing. Do you use it to get ahead on the calculus chapter, or spend it talking?

setting: The break room at whatever part-time job sixteen-year-olds get. A Thursday in November, the fluorescent light doing its flicker thing.
prompt: Your shift supervisor offers you an extra four hours Saturday morning at time-and-a-half. It cuts into the weekend, but it is eighty dollars.
{{new:classmate}} wants to copy your homework. It would take ten seconds to slide it across the desk.
Dad, your father, asks if you want to come along to help him repaint the garage this weekend. It is not mandatory, but he is asking.
Your locker neighbour asks if you want to split the cost of a bus pass for the month. It's $28 each.

setting: The school cafeteria, a Thursday in February. The drama club sign-up sheet has been taped to the pillar by the vending machines.
prompt: Auditions are next week. You have zero experience but {{new:drama_friend}} says that's the point of auditioning.
Mom texts asking if you'll be home for dinner. You already told {{new:friend}} you'd hang out.

setting: Your bedroom, a Sunday evening. The course selection form for junior year is due by noon tomorrow.
prompt: There's a slot for AP Chemistry, which looks good on a transcript, or an elective in woodshop, which actually sounds interesting.
Your mom packed your lunch again. Do you take it or buy from the cafeteria?

setting: Saturday morning. Your dad is in the driveway with a socket set and a 1999 Corolla that belongs to a neighbor.
prompt: He offers to teach you basic car maintenance if you spend the morning helping. You had plans, vague ones, but plans.
Your intro economics professor mentions that the campus tutoring center pays $14 an hour. Your barista shifts already fill three evenings. Do you apply anyway?

setting: The registrar's office, a Wednesday in late August, fluorescent lights and a queue that hasn't moved in twenty minutes.
beat: Declaring a major by the end of week two saves $200 in administrative fees and locks in your advising track.
dialogue: The advisor says undeclared students get the last pick of spring sections, every single semester.
prompt: You had assumed you'd figure this out by Christmas. Committing to business administration now saves money and structure, but it closes off the semester you'd planned to use for looking around.

setting: Group chat, 11 p.m. on a Thursday. Three people you met at orientation want to split a four-bedroom off-campus apartment starting January.
prompt: Moving off campus saves money monthly but empties nearly half your savings before spring semester starts. Do you commit to the apartment?
Mom texts asking if you want her to mail the noise-canceling headphones sitting in your old room. They would take up space but they would also help. Do you say yes?
Your sociology professor mentions that a research assistant position pays $12 an hour. It is Monday. Applications close Friday. Do you apply?

setting: The break room at the coffee shop, a Thursday evening in late September. A typed flyer is taped to the fridge next to a reminder about labelling food.
prompt: A co-worker is quietly organizing a petition asking management for a shift-scheduling policy that gives at least a week's notice. Signing takes thirty seconds and puts your name on a list management will see.
Your mother calls to check in. She mentions she heard the coffee shop is hiring a shift supervisor. You have not told her you already know and are not sure you want it.
Your 8 a.m. lecture conflicts with your best shift at the café. Do you drop the lecture or lose the shift?
Your study group has a group chat. {{new:classmate}} keeps tagging you in memes at 2 a.m. Do you mute the thread or stay in?

setting: The campus financial aid office, a Wednesday in February. A poster on the wall explains the difference between subsidized and unsubsidized loans, using a diagra
prompt: Your aid package for next year has a $4,200 gap. You can take an additional unsubsidized loan or pick up a second part-time shift and probably sleep less.

setting: The back parking lot of the coffee shop where you work, a slow Sunday afternoon in March.
prompt: {{new:coworker}}, who has been here three years longer than you, offers to walk you through a side arrangement: reselling concert tickets bought through the shop's employee presale access. Forty dollars a ticket, clean. Your manager would call it a firing offense.

risk.description: Your manager pulls the presale logs, connects the sales back to your login, and terminates you on the spot, with a note in your file.

prompt: Your mother calls — you haven't spoken in a few weeks — and she mentions Dad has been quieter than usual. She doesn't say worried. She says quieter. Do you call him back today?

Your trade cert sits in a drawer. College is fine, but the guy who graduated your program two years ago is already pulling $28/hr on a union crew. Do you quietly start attending the college's contractor networking nights?
Mom texts out of nowhere — your mother, who has a gift for turning a check-in into a needs-assessment — asking if you are eating properly. Answering honestly would open a longer conversation.

Your trade cert got you the barista job, but the guy on the espresso machine next to you is pulling a philosophy degree and making the same $9 an hour. Do you sign up for a full course load this semester, or keep the hours and the cash?
Your landlord is raising rent by $180 a month starting next quarter. Do you negotiate or start looking?

setting: The break room at work, a Thursday in March. Someone has taped a flyer to the coffee machine about a weekend digital marketing certification bootcamp — two days
prompt: Your marketing coordinator title is already a stretch on your trade background. Does paying $650 to add a certificate line to your résumé feel like investing in yourself, or like paying for permission you already earned?

setting: A Friday lunch — the kind that started as a team thing and ended as you and one other person from the office.
prompt: {{new:coworker}} suggests splitting a two-bedroom across town and cutting both your rents by around $400 each. You have never lived with a stranger from work before.
Your landlord is raising rent by $180 a month starting next month. Do you absorb it or start looking for somewhere cheaper?

Your trade cert is gathering dust behind the marketing degree. A former instructor texts asking if you want weekend shifts installing HVAC units at $38/hr. Do you take the weekend work or protect your off time?

Your mother texts asking if you want her old car. It is a 2009 Corolla with 140,000 miles and what she describes as 'a personality.' Free, but yours to insure and maintain. Do you take it or keep using the bus?
Your apartment building has a rooftop with a better view than anything you paid for. The door is propped open with a brick. Do you go up?
Your $42,000 salary just cleared its first full month. Do you automate $200 into savings or keep it liquid because something will come up?

setting: A Thursday evening, the break room at your office. Someone has taped a printout of the benefits enrollment portal to the fridge.
prompt: Open enrollment closes Friday. The premium health plan costs $87 more a month than the basic one. You are 23 and have been to a doctor twice since high school.

setting: A group chat from your mother, Mom, that begins with three paragraphs about a cousin's wedding before arriving at the actual question.
prompt: Mom wants you to come home for a long weekend, which means six hours of driving, a pull-out couch, and being asked about your five-year plan by your father. You have no five-year plan.
The apartment below yours has a vacancy at $150 less per month than your current place, but your new neighbor's band practices on weeknights. Do you move or stay?
Your landlord is raising rent by $210 a month starting in sixty days. Do you try to negotiate, or start looking for a new place?

Mom, your mother, keeps forwarding real estate listings in your hometown. A two-bed starter place has dropped to $187,000. Do you agree to a viewing, or tell her you are not ready to be that close to home?
Your marketing coordinator title puts you near the bottom of every org chart. A free online certification in Google Analytics lands in your inbox. Do you spend the next three weekends on it?
Your spouse suggests skipping date night again to save the $80. You've cancelled three times this month already.

setting: A Saturday morning in March, the kitchen table covered in printouts from Zillow and a yellow legal pad with numbers that do not quite add up.
prompt: A two-bedroom condo three blocks from work just listed at $312,000. Your pre-approval goes to $340,000, and you have $8,615 in savings. Do you make an offer and stretch, or wait for something you can afford more comfortably?
Your mother calls — your mom, who you haven't spoken to properly in months — and mentions her knee has been swelling since July. She says she didn't want to bother anyone.
Your phone needs replacing. You could get a refurbished model for $180 or put the new one on the company card and call it a business expense.

setting: A Saturday morning in March. Your mother's kitchen, which smells exactly the same as it did when you were twelve.
prompt: Your mother mentions, with studied casualness, that your father's knees are worse and the guttering needs replacing. She is not asking you directly. Do you offer to come back next weekend with your tools, or let the comment land and move on?
A colleague mentions a weekend project management course. $850, nine Saturdays. You already know most of it, but the certificate has the right logo on it.
Your spouse left a half-finished grocery list on the counter. You notice it is in someone else's handwriting.
Your spouse wants to try for a baby. You have been saying 'soon' for two years. Soon is now.

setting: Your mother's kitchen on a Sunday, the same floral placemats from your childhood. She has lost weight since you last visited.
prompt: Your mother, who raised you in this house and has not asked you for a single thing in a decade, mentions she cannot afford the co-pays on her new blood pressure medication. Do you offer to cover it without making it a whole conversation, or ask her to walk you through her finances first?
A gym membership you have been paying $47 a month for since January sits at zero visits. Cancel it or keep paying on the theory that guilt is a valid fitness strategy.
Your spouse has started leaving the bedroom light on until you come to bed. You have been sleeping on the couch for three weeks and neither of you has mentioned it.

setting: A Saturday in March, the kitchen of your parents' house. The cabinet doors still hang slightly wrong, the way they always have.
prompt: Your mother mentions, carefully, that your father has missed two doctor's appointments and she cannot get him to reschedule. She is asking you to be the one who talks to him.
The benefits renewal form has a line for voluntary life insurance. Doubling your coverage adds $38 a month.

Your manager's parking spot sits empty every Friday afternoon. You have been covering his work for three months without a title or a dollar to show for it. Do you put the ask in writing, or keep your head down?
The annual review cycle starts next week. Do you push for a promotion conversation now, or let it ride another year?

setting: A Saturday morning in March. You are at an urgent care clinic two miles from home, waiting behind a man describing his elbow at length to the receptionist.
prompt: Do you book a follow-up with a GP and start taking this seriously, or tell yourself it was just the drive over and let it lapse?

setting: A conference call in January. Three people you have never met from Corporate Restructuring are asking about your team's headcount and what, exactly, a Senior An
prompt: Do you answer carefully and make your function sound indispensable, or be candid about the redundancies and hope transparency reads as trustworthy?
Your mother calls, just to talk. You have not spoken in a while. Do you pick up or call back tomorrow?
Your union rep emails to say the company is offering voluntary early retirement packages to anyone over 60. Do you request the paperwork?
Your knee has been swelling after the commute. The GP says imaging would settle it. Do you book the MRI?
Your spouse wants to book a two-week anniversary trip to Portugal. It would cost roughly $6,400 all in. Do you go?
The office gym membership renews automatically at $67 a month. You have not been in eleven months. Cancel or keep pretending?

setting: A Thursday afternoon in the break room. The company-wide email landed twenty minutes ago and people are re-reading it on their phones rather than each other's f
prompt: Corporate is consolidating two analytics teams. Your position is safe but your team of four is being cut to two. Do you advocate loudly for your people, or stay quiet and protect your own standing?

setting: A Saturday morning in your kitchen. Your mother — who you haven't spoken to in a few months — has sent a voicemail that lasts four minutes and mentions your fat
prompt: Mom's voicemail is hard to decipher but the word 'memory' comes up repeatedly. Do you call her back today, or wait until you can brace yourself properly?
The retirement calculator on your screen says you need $1.4 million. You have $20,764. Do you close the tab or start a budget?
Mom, your mother, calls to say your father's driving has become a problem. He disagrees. She wants you involved. Do you drive out this weekend or suggest they sort it themselves?
Your spouse keeps leaving the retirement calculator open on the shared laptop. Do you sit down and actually run the numbers together, or close the tab and make dinner?
The doctor's office sends a letter about scheduling a routine colonoscopy. You are 61 and two years overdue. Do you call back this week, or let the letter migrate to the recycling bin?
The library is running a free tablet class for seniors on Thursday mornings. Do you sign up, or decide you have managed this long without one?

setting: A Tuesday in March. The cardiologist's waiting room has a small fish tank and magazines from 2019.
prompt: The doctor recommends a cardiac stress test - routine at your age, she says, though the word routine is doing some work. Your co-pay will be $340. Do you schedule it now, or ask to revisit at your next annual?
A neighbor mentions that the HOA is looking for someone to chair the social committee. It is unpaid and reportedly exhausting. Do you volunteer?

setting: A Sunday afternoon phone call. Your mother, Mom, who you have not spoken to in some months, picks up on the second ring.
prompt: She sounds sharp today, sharper than last time, but she mentions twice that she has been eating mostly toast. You could offer to drive up and stay a few days, or send a grocery delivery and call it handled. What kind of child do you want to have been?
Your Tuesday morning is now structurally identical to your Saturday morning. Do you sign up for a community woodworking class to give the week some shape?
A trade magazine arrives — the old one from your working years — and it still lists your former union's annual dinner. Do you go?
A letter from a Medicare supplemental plan arrives, offering slightly better dental coverage for $47 more per month. Do you switch or leave things as they are?
A letter arrives from a company offering to manage your Medicare supplements for a flat monthly fee. The brochure has a lot of eagles on it.

setting: A Tuesday morning in the cardiologist's waiting room, the kind with a fish tank and magazines from eighteen months ago.
prompt: You are already spending more than you earn each year. Do you fill the new prescription immediately, or wait and appeal to insurance first?
A neighbor two doors down has started leaving their trash bins in front of your driveway every collection day. It has been six weeks.

setting: A community centre in late January. Folding chairs, bad coffee, and a sign on the door that says Adult Enrichment.
prompt: It is a small expense you cannot entirely justify. Do you sign up and find out whether you are actually someone who paints, or save the money for something useful?
A letter from Medicare arrives with a correction notice and a $340 bill you do not recognize. Do you call the number on the letter or ignore it?
Your mother calls — her voice thinner than you remember — asking if you might visit this month. Do you book the trip or promise next month instead?
A letter arrives offering a free cruise for two in exchange for attending a ninety-minute resort presentation. Do you send back the reply card?
{{new:best friend}} texts during third period: he has a spare and wants to know if you can meet him at the vending machines. You have a quiz sixth period you have not studied for.
Your mother has left a library book on your bed about summer coding camps. The sticky note says only 'just in case'. You have not asked her opinion on anything career-related in months.
{{new:best friend}} texts asking if you will come watch him play the ukulele at an open mic. He actually bought the ukulele.
The garden center's spring rush is starting. Rick offers you a supervisor role for the season - more hours, more responsibility, same eleven dollars an hour. Do you take it?
There is an open sign-up for the school's winter talent show. You have no discernible talent, which is apparently not a disqualifier based on last year's lineup.
Dad is building something in the shed again and has left the door open, which is new. You could go ask what it is, or let him have the silence he usually prefers.
The vending machine returns your dollar bill three times in a row. You could keep feeding it until it gives you the chips, or pocket the extra two dollars.
{{new:best friend}} invites you to a weekend camping trip with four people you only half know. It costs $60 for your share of the site and food. Do you go?
{{new:manager}} says there are eight more flats of impatiens in the van. You are already twenty minutes past the end of your shift. Do you stay and finish, or clock out on time?
The garden centre wants you back for the spring season. The hours are the same, the polo is still green, and your track commitments are over. Do you re-up?

{{new:best friend}}, your best friend, texts to say he is thinking about dropping out of his electrician programme after one semester. He wants to know what you think. Do you tell him honestly, or tell him it is his call?
The recycling drive grant came through. {{new:classmate}} texts to say your share is $38, not $40 — one volunteer showed up twice and claimed an extra cut. Do you let it go?

setting: The school notice board, a Monday in March. A hand-lettered sign says the library is hiring a part-time shelving assistant at $9.50 an hour, eight hours a week.
prompt: The hours are Tuesdays and Thursdays after school. It would mean $76 a week and a quieter social life. Do you apply, or leave it for someone who needs the money more?

setting: The gym lobby, a Friday evening in April. Varsity season is halfway through and Coach Bell is running a skills clinic open to non-roster students.
prompt: You skipped tryouts in August. The clinic is free and runs three consecutive Saturdays. {{new:best friend}} says it is basically tryout practice for next year. Do you sign up, or close that door quietly?
Your shift at the grocery store ends at nine. The manager asks if you want to pick up Saturday mornings permanently, an extra four hours a week.
{{new:friend}} texts asking if you want to drive out to the reservoir with a few people this Sunday. You do not have a car, which means either getting a ride or telling your mom.

setting: The hallway outside the gym, a Wednesday afternoon. The varsity sign-up sheet from last fall is long gone, but Coach Bell has stopped you specifically.
prompt: Joining now means practice four days a week through May, which is a real cost. Passing means this particular door closes for good.

setting: The school library, a Tuesday in April. {{new:best friend}}, your best friend, has commandeered the corner table with a laptop and a very long list.
prompt: {{new:best friend}} wants help building a website to sell vintage sneakers he sources at estate sales. It will take most of your free evenings for a month, unpaid, in exchange for a cut of whatever it makes.
{{new:best friend}}, your best friend, wants you to skip last period on Friday and take the bus to the mall. Nothing illegal, just time.

setting: The break room at a garden centre, a Saturday in March. There is a laminated sign about hand-washing that nobody has followed.
prompt: It is real money, around $840 a summer month if you stay consistent, but every Saturday gone is a Saturday gone.

setting: The kitchen table, a Sunday in October. Dad, your father, has left the automotive section of the classifieds folded open.
beat: There is a 2003 Civic listed for $1,800. It runs, according to the seller, most of the time.
dialogue: Dad says he will match whatever you save, dollar for dollar, up to eight hundred.
prompt: You have $420 right now. Do you commit to the car fund and start saying no to everything, or keep your money loose and your options open?
Mom, your mother, asks if you want to join her book club discussion this Thursday. One other teenager might be there. Possibly.

setting: The school library, a Tuesday in November. {{new:friend}} has a sign-up sheet and an expression that suggests this matters to her.
prompt: You have never touched a lighting board, but the instructions are apparently two pages and she says you are, quote, the most responsible person she can still ask.
The soccer league has a group chat now. Someone suggests a post-game Tuesday at the bar. You have a 7 a.m. shift Wednesday.

setting: A Wednesday evening in March, the community college registration portal. The spring list of electives is open.
prompt: An Introduction to Business Administration section still has seats. It does not count toward anything you are currently taking, but it runs Tuesday nights and the garden center is closed Tuesdays.
{{new:best friend}} texts asking if you want to carpool to the college library Sunday. You have already read everything due this week.
The garden centre wants you to open three Saturdays in a row. Six a.m. starts. Your knee has been quiet lately, which is probably not an invitation.

setting: A Tuesday evening in September, the community college registration portal timing out for the third time.
prompt: Part-time enrollment would cost $1,400 for two classes and take a full year to get anywhere. Full-time means quitting the garden centre and living on savings. Do you commit to college properly, or test the water with a single night class?

setting: The garden centre break room, a Friday in November. Rick's motivational calendar has been replaced with a new one, same brand, different quotes, same energy.
prompt: The assistant manager position just opened. Fourteen dollars an hour, thirty-five hours a week, which works out to around $25,500 a year. It also means Rick is your direct report, which the posting does not mention but everyone knows.

setting: A Saturday in late July, your bedroom. A community college catalog has materialized on your desk - Mom's handwriting on a sticky note says 'just look.'
prompt: Enrollment for fall is still open. Two years, affordable, and you would still be living at home. Do you look into registering, or let the deadline pass quietly?
The garden center is quiet on a Wednesday and you find a twenty in the break room. No name on it, no one nearby. Do you hand it to Rick or put it in your pocket?
{{new:best friend}}, your best friend, wants you to cover his shift at his family's dry-cleaning counter Saturday. Four hours, no pay, just a favor. Your knee is already unhappy about being vertical.

setting: A Saturday in November, the garden centre break room. Rick has left a motivational calendar on the folding table and someone has crossed out all the quotes.
prompt: More money means more hours on your feet, which the knee will have thoughts about. Do you take the promotion or keep the lighter workload?
Your mom asks if you want to join her grocery run. It is a Saturday with nothing else on it.

setting: The school cafeteria, a Thursday in February. Someone has taped a flyer for the spring talent show to your lunch table.
prompt: {{new:best friend}}, your best friend, wants you both to enter together. He has already written down an act involving a ukulele he does not yet own.

setting: A Friday night in April. {{new:best friend}}, your best friend, is at your door with a bicycle and a vague plan involving the reservoir three miles away.
prompt: It is 9 p.m. and your curfew is 10:30. The ride there and back is tight and the path is unlit after the first quarter mile.

risk.description: The unlit section of path ends abruptly in a drainage ditch and you go over the handlebars at speed.

setting: The community college library, a Wednesday in October. The business programme's notice board has a single index card pinned to it advertising a peer-tutoring st
prompt: Thirty dollars a session, twice a week, to help first-year students with the intro accounting unit you aced last semester. It cuts into your study time but not catastrophically.

{{new:best friend}} texts at midnight. He has found an open mic night that takes spoken-word pieces and says your public-speaking win at the history panel counts as experience. He wants you both to sign up for next Friday. Do you say yes?

setting: A Tuesday evening in January, the kitchen. Your high school diploma is somewhere in a drawer and the community college catalogue is open on the table.
prompt: The two-year business administration programme costs $4,200 per year and would mean being in class four evenings a week. Do you enrol, or stay working and figure out the rest later?

setting: A Saturday in April, the garden centre on Ridgeway, where Mom's friend {{new:manager}} is stacking flats of petunias.
prompt: The weekend job your mom mentioned last year is open again — same green polo, now $11 an hour. You passed before. Do you ask about it this time?
{{new:classmate}} texts at 11 p.m. asking if you can 'look over' his take-home ethics exam before he submits it. You have a midterm of your own tomorrow.

risk.description: A TA who knows you both notices the overlap and files an academic integrity report naming you as a contributor.

setting: The finance club room, a Thursday in January, the whiteboard already covered in someone's cash-flow model from last semester.
prompt: The internship pays $18 an hour and would count toward your credit hours, but it is in-person five days a week starting in May, when you are still technically enrolled.

setting: Your dorm room, a Sunday afternoon in March, {{new:roommate}} out for the weekend.
prompt: She is your closest person and she is asking a real question. You can be honest about the distance and what it costs you, or you can tell her it is an easy yes and mean it.
Your performance-supplement use has crept from exam weeks to most mornings. A friend mentions a campus health clinic that does no-questions consultations on Tuesdays.
The Finance Club sends a ranking of mock-portfolio performance. You finished eleventh out of forty-three. {{new:roommate}} finished third. Do you ask him how he thinks differently, or let it sit?

setting: A Thursday afternoon in early March, the hallway outside your advisor's office. There is a corkboard with three internship flyers and a sign reminding you that
prompt: A summer analyst role at a regional investment firm is posted — unpaid, but it would put a real line on your résumé. Taking it means giving up the paid campus research position you were counting on to chip at your debt.

setting: A Monday morning in late April, your college email inbox. The subject line reads: 'Scholarship Reference — Verification Request.'
prompt: The scholarship committee has sent a follow-up to the reference you wrote for {{new:classmate}}, your classmate, asking you to confirm, in writing, that nothing in the application misrepresents his academic record. Signing the form means restating what you already said. You have seen his work up close.

{{new:best friend}} calls on a Sunday asking if she can list you as a guarantor on her new apartment lease. She has never missed a payment on anything. The liability would be up to $14,400 if she defaulted.
{{new:roommate}} borrowed your charger three days ago and you need it back. He has headphones on.

setting: The finance club's Thursday meeting room, November, a whiteboard still showing someone else's arbitrage diagram.
prompt: You have forty minutes a night to prepare. Do you grind the technical research and compete seriously, or show up, participate minimally, and save the hours?
{{new:best friend}}, your best friend, wants a second opinion on a text she is about to send her ex. It is not a good text.
{{new:classmate}}, your classmate, texts asking if you still have the grant-proposal outline from last semester. You have it. He is not in the same class anymore.
Your phone has 6 percent battery and the charger is across campus. A stranger offers to charge it at their table at the café, leaving it unwatched for twenty minutes.

risk.description: They have gone when you return, but the phone is still there and fully charged - and they left a note with their number.

setting: Your dorm room, a Sunday night in November. Your mom — you have barely spoken since move-in — has left a voicemail that is three minutes and twenty seconds long
prompt: The voicemail is about the notebooks, but three minutes is about something else. Do you call back tonight, or let it sit until you have figured out what you actually want to say?

setting: A Saturday in late August, the folding table outside the college registrar's office. The line has not moved in forty minutes.
prompt: Committing early locks in a cohort and an advisor; undecided buys time but puts you at the back of the queue for limited lab sections.

setting: A Sunday in October, a video call with {{new:best friend}}, your best friend, who has ended up at a college four hours away.
prompt: {{new:best friend}} wants to visit next weekend. You have a midterm Monday morning and she has never once let a weekend stay land on fewer than two late nights.

{{new:classmate}}, your classmate from high school, messages asking you to be a reference for a scholarship he is applying to. The application asks if you have ever seen him misrepresent his work. You have.
{{new:best friend}} texts at 11 p.m. asking if you did the AP Environmental Science reading. You did. She did not.

setting: The kitchen, a Thursday evening in April. A thick envelope from a state university sits next to a thin one from a private college.
prompt: The state school is offering a partial scholarship — $4,200 a year. The private college costs twice as much but has the research program your AP Science teacher spent two paragraphs recommending. Do you follow the money or follow the program?

setting: A move-in weekend in late August, a dorm hallway stacked with flat-pack furniture and someone else's amp.
prompt: Your assigned roommate, {{new:roommate}}, has already claimed the window desk and put up a poster that is going to bother you every day for nine months. Do you say something now or let it go and pick your battles later?
A campus org is selling $6 raffle tickets for a $400 prize. You have $1,440 and a memory of penciling five dollars into a winter formal betting pool.

risk.description: Your second ticket wins the draw. You collect $400 from a woman who looks genuinely disappointed to hand it over.

prompt: {{new:best friend}} texts asking if you can cover her shift at a frozen yogurt place this Saturday. You have never worked there, but she says the owner will not notice.

setting: The AP Environmental Science room, a Tuesday in January. Your teacher stops you on the way out.
prompt: It means three Saturdays in February helping compile data. No pay, but your teacher writes the recommendations that get people into good schools.
The calculus teacher assigns seats for the midterm review and you end up next to {{new:classmate}}, who is clearly going to ask to copy your notes.

setting: A Sunday afternoon in February, the living room, Dad watching a game with the sound low.
prompt: He is not angry, exactly, but the air in the room has a specific texture. Do you sit down and watch the rest of the game with him, or find somewhere else to be?
{{new:best friend}} wants to split a $14 pizza after school. Your calculus test is tomorrow.
A classmate asks to copy your calculus homework. They say they will owe you one.

setting: The school corridor, a Friday morning. A notice on the bulletin board advertises a paid summer internship at the local library: $10 an hour, twelve weeks.
prompt: Applications close in two weeks. It would mean giving up the unscheduled summer you have been looking forward to, but it is real money and something to put on a resume.
{{new:best friend}}, your best friend, texts asking if you want to walk to school tomorrow instead of taking the bus. It adds twenty minutes each way.
There is a blank page at the back of the calculus notes where someone has started a betting pool on the winter formal king result. Your name is already penciled in as an option.

setting: Friday afternoon, the school parking lot, a folding table with a hand-lettered sign reading WINTER CONCERT VOLUNTEERS.
prompt: You already gave up last Saturday for the extra shift. Do you volunteer the next three, or protect the time you have left?

setting: Sunday morning, the living room, Dad — your father — reading something on his phone with the particular expression that means he has an idea.
prompt: Dad says he found a free online typing course and wants the two of you to work through it together on Sunday mornings. It is not the worst idea, but it is your only real morning off.
{{new:best friend}}, your best friend, wants you to ditch last period to walk to the lake. It is a Wednesday.

setting: The break room at a garden centre, a Saturday in March. The laminated schedule has your name on it every weekend through June.
prompt: The owner offers you a regular weekend shift at $9.50 an hour, cash, starting next week. It is steady, dull, and cuts into everything else.
Mom asks if you want to join the family gym membership. She will cover your share, but you owe her two hours of yard work a month.

setting: A folding table in the school gymnasium, a Thursday in November. The sign says SPRING ELECTIVE SIGN-UP.
prompt: The art elective fills fast and looks easy. The AP Environmental Science course is harder but the teacher has a reputation for writing strong college recommendations.
The library internship offer arrives: nine weeks, $10 an hour, weekday mornings. Accepting means deferring your college orientation week by one session.
